title: Structural geology & tectonics
sub: Lecture 7 · 16 Nov · weekly test at the next lecture + final exam
blurb: Stress and strain, brittle vs ductile, joints, faults and folds, plates and mantle convection, the three plate boundaries, the subduction factory and the Wilson cycle.
h1: Structural geology and tectonics, one step at a time
lede: Two halves. First **structural geology**: how stress deforms rock, and the structures that result (joints, faults, veins, folds, foliation). Then **tectonics**: rigid plates moved by mantle convection, what happens at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries, and the Wilson cycle that opens and closes oceans.
six: **Stress** = force per unit area; **strain** = the change it causes. When stress is greater than the rock's **internal strength**, the rock deforms.

**Brittle**: 0–15 km, below ~300 °C, low pressure, fast → **joints** (no displacement), **faults** (displacement), **veins** (filled). **Ductile**: deeper than ~10 km, above ~300 °C → **folds**, **foliation**.
Faults: **normal** = hanging wall down (tension); **reverse** = up (compression); **thrust** = reverse at a low angle; **strike-slip** = sideways (shear).
Rigid **plates** move a few cm per year on the asthenosphere, driven by **mantle convection**. **Divergent** = tension, **convergent** = compression, **transform** = shear.
Subduction makes **arcs** (andesite, diorite) and **paired metamorphism** (blueschist–eclogite + greenschist–amphibolite–granulite). The **Wilson cycle** = repeated opening and closing of oceans.
mockNote: Questions come from the lecture 7 slides and the teacher's explanations in the recording.
foot: Sources: lecture 7 slides "Structural geology and tectonics" (Mgr. Václav Santolík, PhD, CZU) and your Wispr recordings of 16 Nov 2026 (two parts). Lines marked "recording" were said in class but are not on the slides. The recording is poor in places ("fold" = fault, "roof wall" = foot wall, "astrosphere" = asthenosphere, "equationary origin" = accretionary orogen), so the slide wording is used.

questions.q: Which field studies deformational features in rocks, from outcrop to regional scale?
questions.h: The smallest of the three scales.
questions.e: Structural geology = outcrop to regional. Tectonics = regional to global. Earth structure = global.

questions.q: Which field studies large-scale plate interactions, from regional to global scale?
questions.e: Tectonics looks at plates: regional to global scale.

questions.q: What does structural geology study?
questions.answer: The architecture of the Earth's crust and the processes responsible for its deformation
wrong: The history of life through fossils
Only the deep core of the Earth
questions.e: That is the slide definition.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a reason to study structural geology?
questions.e: The slide lists: reconstructing the history of a rock or region, geomorphology, natural resource exploration, geohazard assessment and building foundations.

questions.q: What is stress?
questions.answer: The force exerted per unit area
wrong: The physical change of a rock
The amount of water in a rock
questions.e: Stress = force per unit area. The change it causes is strain.

questions.q: What is strain?
questions.answer: The physical change that results in response to stress
wrong: The force exerted per unit area
The ability of a rock to resist stress
questions.e: Strain is the response; stress is the cause.

questions.q: What is deformation?
questions.answer: Any change in a rock's shape, position or orientation due to stress
wrong: Only the breaking of a rock
The weathering of a rock at the surface
questions.e: Deformation is the general term. It includes moving and rotating a rock, not only changing its shape.

questions.q: When does a rock deform?
questions.answer: When the applied stress is greater than its internal strength
wrong: When the internal strength is greater than the stress
Only when it is heated above 1000 °C
questions.e: When applied stress is greater than the internal strength of a rock, strain results in the form of deformation.

questions.q: What controls a rock's internal strength?
questions.answer: Composition, temperature, pressure and strain rate
questions.e: All four are on the slide.

questions.q: Which type of stress pulls in opposite directions?
questions.e: Tensional = pulling apart. Compressional = pushing together. Shear = sliding past.

questions.q: What is shear stress?
questions.answer: Transverse forces that make blocks slide past each other
questions.e: Shear = transverse forces. At plate scale it belongs to transform boundaries.

questions.q: Which type of strain is reversible after the stress is released?
questions.e: Elastic strain disappears when the stress is removed. Ductile and brittle are permanent.

questions.q: What happens to a material in brittle strain?
wrong: It changes shape permanently without breaking
It returns to its original shape
questions.e: Brittle = fractures. Ductile = permanent change of shape without breaking.

questions.q: What happens to a material in ductile strain?
wrong: It returns to its original shape
questions.e: Ductile = bends or flows and stays changed.

questions.q: A high strain rate (fast deformation) favours which behaviour?
questions.e: High strain rate → brittle. High temperature and high pressure → ductile.

questions.q: High temperature and high pressure favour which behaviour?
questions.e: Hot, deep rock bends instead of breaking.

questions.q: What is a joint?
questions.answer: A planar fracture with no visible displacement
wrong: A planar fracture along which displacement has occurred
questions.e: Joint = no displacement. Fault = displacement. Vein = filling.

questions.q: What is a fault?
questions.answer: A planar fracture along which displacement has occurred
wrong: A planar fracture with no visible displacement
A planar fabric of aligned micas
questions.e: Along a fault the two sides moved: layers no longer line up.

questions.q: What is a vein?
questions.answer: A fracture filling formed when minerals precipitate from fluids in open cracks
questions.e: Veins are fillings of fractures.

questions.q: Which minerals do veins mostly contain, according to the teacher?
questions.e: Mostly quartz or calcite, sometimes with ores such as gold.

questions.q: What are the typical depth and temperature of brittle deformation?
questions.e: Brittle: 0–15 km, below ~300 °C, low confining pressure, higher strain rate.

questions.q: Which conditions favour brittle deformation?
questions.answer: Low confining pressure and a higher strain rate
wrong: High confining pressure and a lower strain rate
questions.e: Brittle is shallow, cool, low pressure, fast.

questions.q: In a fault, which block is the hanging wall?
questions.e: Hanging wall = upper block, foot wall = lower block. Miners hung their lantern on the upper one.

questions.q: What is a fault scarp?
questions.answer: A steep slope or cliff on the surface created by a fault
wrong: The lower block of a fault
questions.e: Scarp = the step at the surface. Fault line = where the fault plane meets the surface.

questions.q: What is the fault line?
questions.answer: Where the fault plane intersects the surface
wrong: A steep cliff on the surface
The deepest point of the fault
questions.e: Fault line = intersection of the fault plane with the surface.

questions.q: In a normal fault, the hanging wall moves...
questions.e: Normal = extension, hanging wall down.

questions.q: In a reverse fault, the hanging wall moves...
questions.e: Reverse = compression, hanging wall up.

questions.q: What is a thrust fault?
questions.answer: A reverse fault with a low angle (almost horizontal)
wrong: A normal fault with a steep angle
A fault where blocks move sideways
questions.e: Thrust = compression, hanging wall up, low angle. The exact angle is not needed.

questions.q: Which fault forms under shear stress, with blocks moving laterally?
questions.e: Strike-slip = shear, sideways movement. Typical for transform boundaries.

questions.q: What is a fold?
questions.answer: Curved or bent layers formed by ductile bending
questions.e: Folds are ductile; joints, faults and veins are brittle.

questions.q: Which fold has an arch shape (∩)?
questions.e: Anticline = arch ∩. Syncline = U.

questions.q: Which fold is U-shaped, like a valley?
questions.e: Syncline = U. On the slide: syncline convex (U), anticline concave (∩).

questions.q: What is foliation?
questions.answer: A planar fabric from aligned platy or elongate minerals, or compositional layering, formed during ductile deformation
questions.e: Foliation is a ductile structure, for example aligned micas.

questions.q: Which foliation is wavy planar with aligned mica, at medium grade?
questions.e: Slaty cleavage = low grade, schistosity = medium, gneissic banding = high.

questions.q: Which foliation shows compositional segregation at high grade?
questions.e: Gneissic banding: light and dark bands, high grade.

questions.q: What are the typical conditions of ductile deformation?
questions.answer: Deeper than about 10 km, above about 300 °C, high confining pressure
wrong: 0–15 km, below about 300 °C, low confining pressure
questions.e: Ductile: >~10 km, >~300 °C, high confining pressure, lower strain rate → folding.

questions.q: What is the typical result of ductile deformation?
questions.e: Brittle → fracturing and faulting. Ductile → folding.

questions.q: What is geomorphology?
questions.answer: The science of how Earth's surface landscapes are formed and changed by natural processes
wrong: The study of the Earth's core
questions.e: That is the slide definition.

questions.q: Which landscape example shows folded layers forming long parallel ridges and valleys?
questions.answer: The Ridge and Valley section of the Appalachians
wrong: The Great Rift Valley in East Africa
questions.e: Appalachians = folds. The East African Rift = extension.

questions.q: How fast do tectonic plates move?
questions.e: A few cm per year, about the speed your fingernails grow.

questions.q: How is the motion of plates measured today?
questions.e: GPS stations measure plate motion directly.

questions.q: What drives plate motion?
questions.e: Mantle rock is heated near the core, rises, cools and sinks again. The plates float on the viscous asthenosphere.

questions.q: Which boundary is matched with the right stress?
questions.answer: Divergent = tension, convergent = compression, transform = shear
wrong: Divergent = compression, convergent = tension, transform = shear
Divergent = shear, convergent = compression, transform = tension
questions.e: Plates moving apart = extension, colliding = compression, sliding past = horizontal shear.

questions.q: What is the main stress regime at a divergent boundary?
questions.e: Plates move apart: tension, normal faults.

questions.q: Which rocks form when the upper mantle melts at a divergent boundary?
questions.e: Mantle melting gives mafic magma: gabbro below the surface, basalt on it.

questions.q: Where does new oceanic crust form?
questions.e: Divergent boundary in oceanic crust = mid-ocean ridge, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East Pacific Rise.

questions.q: Which is an example of a continental rift?
questions.e: Continental rifts: East African Rift and the Eger Rift (Czechia, 18 Ma).

questions.q: In the opening of an ocean, which example is the young, narrow ocean between the rift valley and the wide ocean basin?
questions.e: Rift valley (East Africa) → young ocean (Red Sea) → ocean basin (Atlantic).

questions.q: Why does the oceanic plate subduct beneath the continental plate?
questions.answer: Oceanic plate is denser; continental plate is more buoyant
wrong: The ocean water pushes it down
questions.e: Denser oceanic lithosphere sinks under buoyant continental lithosphere.

questions.q: What forms where an oceanic plate meets another oceanic plate?
wrong: An orogenic belt from continental collision
questions.e: Ocean × ocean = intra-oceanic subduction = island arc.

questions.q: The Andes are an example of which setting?
questions.e: Oceanic plate beneath a continent forms a continental arc (accretionary orogen).

questions.q: Which magmatism is typical for both island arcs and continental arcs?
questions.answer: Andesitic volcanism and dioritic to granodioritic plutonism
questions.e: Subduction magma is mainly intermediate.

questions.q: What is paired metamorphism at a subduction zone?
questions.answer: High P/T (blueschist–eclogite) together with medium P/T (greenschist–amphibolite–granulite)
wrong: Low P/T together with no metamorphism
questions.e: High P/T in the subducting plate, medium P/T in the upper plate.

questions.q: In the subduction factory, what do earthquakes follow?
questions.e: Earthquakes get deeper the further they are from the trench, tracing the sinking plate.

questions.q: What forms where two continental plates collide?
questions.e: Continental collision: orogenic belts such as the Alps and Himalayas, with thrusting, folding and regional metamorphism.

questions.q: Which magmatism is typical for continental collision?
questions.e: The slide: plutonic magmatism (not much volcanic).

questions.q: Which is true of transform boundaries?
questions.answer: Strike-slip faults and earthquakes, but no significant metamorphism or magmatism
wrong: Strong magmatism and new oceanic crust
questions.e: Plates slide past each other: strike-slip faults, earthquakes.

questions.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of which boundary?
questions.e: A transform boundary with a strike-slip fault.

questions.q: How do Hawaii's volcanoes form, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: From a mantle plume in the middle of a plate (a hotspot)
questions.e: Hotspots are not at plate boundaries: magma rises from deep in the mantle.

questions.q: What does the Wilson cycle describe?
questions.answer: The repeated opening and closing of ocean basins
wrong: The movement of the magnetic poles
questions.e: The Wilson cycle is the life cycle of plate tectonics.

questions.q: Which order matches the Wilson cycle?
questions.answer: Rift → young ocean → ocean basin → subduction → continental collision
wrong: Collision → rift → subduction → ocean basin → young ocean
Ocean basin → rift → collision → young ocean → subduction
Subduction → rift → collision → ocean basin → young ocean
questions.e: An ocean opens (rift, young ocean, ocean basin), then closes (subduction, collision); erosion and a new rift restart it.

questions.q: What will you do in the next practical?
questions.answer: Make a poster on a chosen region's structures and tectonics, using AI, in teams of two or three
questions.e: Bring scissors and markers.

questions.q: Compression at shallow depth, where rocks are brittle. Which structure forms?
questions.e: Compression pushes the hanging wall up: a reverse (or thrust) fault. Slide 21 activity.

questions.q: Tension at shallow depth, where rocks are brittle. Which structure forms?
questions.e: Tension pulls the blocks apart and the hanging wall drops down: a normal fault. Slide 21 activity.

questions.q: Compression at greater depth, where rocks deform by ductile flow. What forms?
questions.e: Deep and hot, the rock bends instead of breaking: folds. Slide 21 activity.

questions.q: Shear stress acting on a large region at depth (ductile) produces a...
questions.e: Teacher said: shear over large regions makes a shear zone; at the surface the same stress gives strike-slip faults.

questions.q: Why does an earthquake happen?
questions.answer: Stored elastic strain is released in a sudden rupture
wrong: The plate slowly bends by ductile flow
questions.e: Teacher said: plates build up stress as elastic strain, then it is released by a sudden movement along the plate.

questions.q: According to the teacher, why are plate boundaries so interesting for geologists?
questions.answer: Most rocks, many ores, geohazards and volcanism are found there
wrong: They are the only places with sedimentary rocks
Plates are not rigid there, so nothing is measured
They are always in the middle of a plate
questions.e: Plate boundaries are sites of deformation, earthquakes and magmatism (slide 29); the teacher added rocks, ores and geohazards.

questions.q: How deep can a subducted plate sink, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: In some cases down to the core
wrong: Only to the base of the crust
It always melts at the trench
questions.e: Geologists follow sunken plates inside the Earth to read the history of subduction.

questions.q: In a continental arc like the Andes, the intermediate magma forms...
questions.e: Subduction factory: large plutons and volcanoes of intermediate composition (slide 35); the teacher called the big plutons batholiths.

vocab.meaning: The branch of geology that studies the architecture of the Earth's crust and the processes responsible for its deformation. Scale: outcrop to regional.
The study of large-scale plate interactions. Scale: regional to global.
The science of how Earth's surface landscapes are formed and changed by natural processes.
The force exerted per unit area.
The physical change that results in response to stress.
Any change in a rock's shape, position or orientation due to stress.
The ability of a rock to resist deformation under stress, controlled by composition, temperature, pressure and strain rate.
How fast a rock deforms. A higher strain rate favours brittle behaviour.
Pressure acting equally in all directions (lithostatic pressure). High confining pressure favours ductile behaviour.
Pulling in opposite directions.
Pushing together.
Transverse forces: blocks slide past each other.
Reversible: the rock returns to its shape after the stress is released.
The material changes its shape permanently without breaking.
The material fractures.
A planar fracture along which there has been no visible displacement.
A planar fracture along which displacement has occurred.
A fracture filling formed when minerals precipitate from fluids in open cracks; mostly quartz or calcite.
The plane of displacement.
The upper block of a fault.
The lower block of a fault.
Where the fault plane intersects the surface.
A steep slope or cliff on the surface created by a fault.
Extension: the hanging wall moves down.
Compression: the hanging wall moves up.
Compression: the hanging wall moves up, but at a low angle (almost horizontal).
Shear stress: the blocks move laterally (sideways) past each other.
Curved or bent layers formed by ductile bending.
A fold with an arch shape (∩). The slide calls it concave.
A U-shaped fold, like a valley. The slide calls it convex.
A large region where shear stress has deformed the rock.
One of the rigid pieces the lithosphere is broken into; rigid inside, deformed at its boundaries.
Mantle rock heated near the core rises, cools near the surface and sinks again; it drives plate motion.
Plates move apart: crustal extension (tension).
Plates converge and collide: crustal compression.
Plates slide past each other: horizontal shear.
One plate is dragged down beneath another into the mantle.
A valley formed where a continent is pulled apart (continental rift), e.g. the East African Rift.
A divergent boundary in oceanic crust where new oceanic crust forms, e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
An oceanic plate subducting beneath another oceanic plate; forms an island arc.
A chain of volcanic islands formed by intra-oceanic subduction.
Ocean–continent subduction: an oceanic plate beneath a continental plate, as in the Andes.
The belt of volcanoes and plutons formed by ocean–continent subduction; an accretionary orogen.
Two continental plates collide and form orogenic (mountain) belts.
A mountain belt formed by orogeny (mountain building).
Subduction zones as producers of magmatism, paired metamorphism and earthquakes.
High P/T (blueschist–eclogite) in the subducting plate together with medium P/T (greenschist–amphibolite–granulite) in the upper plate.
Volcanism in the middle of a plate above a mantle plume, e.g. Hawaii.
The repeated opening and closing of ocean basins through plate tectonic processes.

{Compressional|Tensional|Shear|Elastic} stress pushes rock together.
{Shear|Tensional|Compressional|Confining} stress is made of transverse forces.

A {fault|joint|vein|fold} is a planar fracture along which displacement has occurred.

Brittle deformation happens at depths of about {0–15|10–50|100–200|0–1} km.
Brittle deformation happens below about {300|30|1000|3000} °C.
Brittle deformation happens under {low|high|extreme|infinite} confining pressure.
The {hanging wall|foot wall|fault plane|fault line} is the upper block of a fault.
The {foot wall|hanging wall|fault scarp|fault plane} is the lower block of a fault.

In a {normal|reverse|thrust|strike-slip} fault the hanging wall moves down.
In a {reverse|normal|strike-slip|transform} fault the hanging wall moves up.
A {thrust|normal|strike-slip|transform} fault is a reverse fault with a low angle.
A {strike-slip|normal|reverse|thrust} fault forms under shear stress.
The two main ductile structures are folds and {foliation|joints|faults|veins}.
An {anticline|syncline|joint|scarp} is a fold with an arch shape.
A {syncline|anticline|thrust|vein} is a U-shaped fold.

{Schistosity|Slaty cleavage|Gneissic banding|Jointing} is wavy planar foliation with mica alignment.

Plate motion is measured using {GPS|thermometers|barometers|compasses}.
Plates are driven by mantle {convection|rotation|tides|wind}.

At a {transform|divergent|convergent|rift} boundary the plates slide past each other.
